title: Imaging the vacuum fluctuations of a quantum field
authors: Yansheng Zhang, Feiyang Wang, Yi Jiang, Alexander C. Jenkins, Paul H. C. Wong, Christoph Eigen, Gehrig Carlse, Zoran Hadzibabic
abstract: Heisenberg uncertainties lead to inevitable fluctuations in the measurement outcomes for quantum-mechanical observables. For quantum fields, these uncertainties result in random spatial structures in snapshots of a field, even when the field is in its ground (vacuum) state. Such `vacuum fluctuations' are at the heart of a wide range of phenomena, from spontaneous decay processes to the Casimir force and Hawking radiation. Their existence is a key manifestation of the quantumness of the physical world, but usually it is only their consequences that are directly observed. Here, we directly observe spatial vacuum fluctuations of a bosonic quantum field. Our experiments are based on a homogeneous planar atomic Bose--Einstein condensate. The condensate comprises two coherently coupled interacting components (spin states), and the quantum field describes its spin degrees of freedom. In the regime where the interactions dominate over the coherent coupling, our system emulates a (massive relativistic) sine-Gordon field. Images of the field reveal simultaneous fluctuations on different length scales, with scale-dependent amplitudes consistent with theoretical predictions for a vacuum state. Observing such fluctuations in the sine-Gordon limit opens many possibilities for laboratory simulations of relativistic fields in regimes that are presently not theoretically tractable.
summary: This research reports the direct experimental observation of spatial vacuum fluctuations in a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate. By tuning the system into a regime emulating a sine-Gordon field, the authors measured fluctuation spectra that match theoretical predictions for the quantum vacuum state. This work establishes the BEC as a powerful quantum simulator for studying fundamental quantum field phenomena.
main_problem: The paper aims to directly observe and measure the spatial vacuum fluctuations of a quantum field, which are fundamental manifestations of quantum mechanics.
main_result: The measured spectrum of fluctuations agrees with theoretical predictions for a vacuum state, confirming the existence of these quantum correlations in the laboratory setting.
method: The experiment uses in-situ state-selective imaging on a Bose-Einstein condensate to measure the structure factor and fluctuation correlations of the spin degrees of freedom.
model_or_system: The physical system is a homogeneous planar atomic Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of $^{39}	ext{K}$ atoms with two coherently coupled spin components. The system's dynamics are modeled to emulate a massive relativistic sine-Gordon field in the appropriate interaction regime.
key_observables: Fluctuations in the relative phase ($\delta\phi$) and population imbalance ($\delta Z$), and the structure factor $S(k)$.
important_parameters: The study explores different regimes, including the Rabi regime and the Josephson regime, and compares vacuum fluctuation scaling ($\propto \omega^{-1}_k$) against thermal fluctuation scaling ($\propto \omega^{-2}_k$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to decouple spin and density dynamics and must account for the attenuation of measured correlations due to imperfect atom detection efficiency ($\gamma < 1$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the concept of vacuum fluctuations and the experimental setup using BEC spin degrees of freedom. Figure 2 shows the time evolution of fluctuations after a quench, comparing classical and quantum evolution.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the theoretical necessity of observing vacuum fluctuations, details the experimental platform (BEC spin dynamics), presents measurements across different parameter regimes (Rabi vs. Josephson), and finally analyzes the measured fluctuation spectra against theoretical predictions.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controlled, tabletop platform to simulate and verify predictions from quantum field theory regarding vacuum structure, which is typically only accessible in extreme astrophysical environments.

In a uniform system, fluctuations of a quantum field ψ (black), here illustrated in one spatial dimension, can be decomposed into plane-wave normal modes (colors) with wave vectors k. Each such mode is equivalent to a quantum harmonic oscillator with a k-dependent frequency ωk, (generalized) displacement xk and momentum pk, and a potential Uk ∝ω2 kx2 k. Even in its ground state, each oscillator exhibits quantum uncertainties; the color shading indicates Gaussian xk uncertainties ∝1/√ωk. (b) The experiment.
